title.title: Alperin's weight conjecture for every block of every group
title.subtitle: Claim: $l(B)$ equals the number of $B$-weights, for every $p$-block, without the classification

plain: A way to count a finite group's building blocks by looking only near one prime, claimed always right

beats.text: The proof's chain, after the paper's own dependency figure
Both sides become counts of tuples with $[x,y]u_1 \cdots u_n = 1$
No classification of finite simple groups: Theorem 3.1 carries the weight

steps: Rewrite both sides as counts of solutions to one group equation
Leftover terms must be divisible by high powers of p
Curves in characteristic p prove that divisibility

achievement.label: Alperin's weight conjecture (1986)
achievement.context: Before: $p$-solvable, symmetric groups, $\mathrm{GL}_n$, many Lie-type groups; reduced to simple groups
achievement.note: Classification-free; Theorem 3.1 is the step an expert should check

verify.detail: No Lean: an AlperinWeights folder exists, but no main result for this family
verify.ourCheck: We read the claim and the review; we did not check the proof

voice.text: Alperin's weight count was known case by case, using the classification of simple groups.
Turn both sides into tuple counts; curves in characteristic p give the divisibility.
Claimed: every block, with no classification.

sources.quote: Alperin's 1986 conjecture counts the simple modular representations in a $p$-block of a finite group locally
then needs a uniform $p$-power divisibility of those counts (its Theorem 3.1)
Theorem 3.1 is the step I would ask an expert to check
Lean dir OAI/RepresentationTheory/AlperinWeights exists but no main_results entry for this family. 59 pp.
